Chapter 6. Evaluating GenAI Applications with MLflow

By this point, you have a tool-calling agent that does more than answer questions. It shows its work. You can inspect the trace, follow the retrieval steps, and see how the final response was produced. That is a strong foundation, but observability is only half the picture. The real question is whether a change actually makes the application better.

For classical machine learning, that question is often answered with a small set of familiar metrics. Generative AI is less tidy. A response can be accurate but unhelpful, fluent but unsafe, or impressive in isolation and unreliable in practice. Quality has several dimensions, and so do the trade-offs around latency and cost.

This is where evaluation becomes a first-class part of the workflow. In MLflow 3.x, evaluation is part of the same system that tracks prompts, code, data, and traces. In this chapter, we show how to build a practical evaluation stack for the Unity Airways assistant: how to create and version evaluation datasets, define meaningful scorers, capture human feedback, and compare a candidate against a baseline. By the end, you will have a repeatable way to decide what is ready to move forward and what still needs work.

The MLflow Evaluation Framework

The evaluation framework in MLflow 3.x provides a structured, traceable, and reproducible way to measure the quality of GenAI applications. It brings together four building blocks:

Datasets

These are the base of every evaluation. Each dataset is a versioned table of examples that represent how users interact with your system, with data points such as query, expected answer, policy reference, intent, and difficulty.

Scorers

These are evaluation functions that assess the quality of your GenAI application outputs. There are two main types of scorers: LLM judges and code-based scorers. Both types of scorers can be combined in a single evaluation. Code-based scorers provide objectivity, while the LLM judges capture meaning and nuance that rules miss. For example, if the Unity Airways assistant says, “Sure, we fly to Mars next Tuesday,” a regex will not save you. A groundedness scorer might.

Evaluation run

This is the execution phase that brings datasets and scorers together. Each run applies one or more scorers to a selected dataset against a candidate build. Results are tracked in MLflow with complete lineage to the candidate version and trace data.

Feedback

This records quality assessments of GenAI application outputs. It standardizes results from automated checks, LLM judges, and human reviewers, storing them on the trace so evidence, rationale, and scores remain linked and comparable over time.

These components work together as a continuous system, ensuring that each change in your application can be tested, compared, and explained using a shared vocabulary and consistent logging standards.

Evaluation Harness

In MLflow, the evaluation harness provides a repeatable way to test and benchmark GenAI applications. Rather than checking outputs case by case, it lets you run the same evaluation workflow systematically: supply test inputs, invoke the application or component under test, apply scorers, and record the results. This makes evaluation consistent, comparable, and reproducible.

Because the harness is integrated with MLflow tracking and tracing, evaluation results stay connected to the code, prompt, data, and traces that produced them. That connection helps bridge offline experimentation and production monitoring, so the same evaluation logic can be reused across development, staging, and production.

Figure 6-1 shows this evaluation loop at a high level. Evaluation datasets feed candidate systems and scorers, evaluation runs produce structured results, and those results link back to traces, versions, and lineage for inspection and debugging.

The mlflow.genai.evaluate() function is the entry point for this workflow. It supports evaluation of:

  • Complete application outputs, such as an agent’s final response

  • Intermediate components, such as retrievers, rerankers, or tools

  • Static datasets or deterministic functions, when predictions are already available

Streaming responses can be consolidated into a single value before scoring, and intermediate steps can be evaluated because MLflow traces preserve structured information about what happened inside the application. Instead of leaving you with an isolated table of metrics, MLflow attaches scores directly to runs and traces, making it easier to compare candidates, investigate failures, and understand regressions.

Evaluation Modes

MLflow supports two evaluation modes, direct evaluation and answer-sheet evaluation, which we will use throughout this chapter.

Direct evaluation

In this mode, MLflow directly calls your GenAI application to generate and evaluate traces. You can achieve this by either wrapping your application’s entry point in a Python function, predict_fn(); or, if your app is deployed as a Databricks model serving endpoint, by wrapping that endpoint in to_predict_fn().

By directly invoking your application, this method allows you to reuse the same scorers defined for offline evaluation in production monitoring, ensuring consistent evaluation. Application input data, your application code (predict_fn), and selected scorers are provided as inputs to mlflow.genai.evaluate(), as seen in Figure 6-2. This function runs the application and scorers concurrently, recording outputs as traces and feedback.

Answer-sheet evaluation

In this mode, the GenAI application is not invoked during evaluation. Instead, you provide precomputed outputs with optional expectations or existing traces, which is referred to as an “answer sheet,” for assessment. MLflow then compares each candidate output against these reference results, making this mode well suited for regression testing, benchmarking, and promotion decisions based on curated production traces.

For instance, if you already have generated outputs and only need to score them, you can provide the corresponding inputs and outputs. The evaluation harness will then apply the configured scorers and log as an MLflow evaluation run.

As Figure 6-3 shows, you provide evaluation data and selected scorers as inputs to mlflow.genai.evaluate(). The evaluation data can include either existing traces or pairs of inputs and precomputed outputs. When inputs and outputs are provided, mlflow.genai.evaluate() automatically constructs traces from them. In both cases, the function runs the specified scorers on each trace, producing feedback for every scorer-trace combination and logging the results as part of the evaluation run.

Creating and Managing Evaluation Datasets

Let’s begin by creating a reliable evaluation dataset. For a GenAI application, that usually means collecting examples that reflect real usage and organizing them in a form that can be reused across evaluation runs.

You can build this dataset from three practical sources already available in your workflow: production traces that capture live user queries, development traces from controlled testing, and a smaller set of synthetic examples that target known edge cases or failure modes. In this section, we show how to assemble these examples into a versioned evaluation dataset in MLflow so the same cases can be used consistently for testing, comparison, and review.

What a GenAI Evaluation Dataset Looks Like

An evaluation dataset should reflect the kinds of questions your application is expected to handle. It is not something you create once and forget. As you collect production traces, review failures, and add new edge cases, the dataset should evolve with the application. Over time, it becomes a working test set: representative enough to catch regressions, but still small and focused enough to inspect and maintain.

For direct evaluation, the dataset schema is simple. Each row contains an inputs dictionary and, optionally, an expectations dictionary. The inputs field holds the data passed into predict_fn(). The expectations field holds ground truth labels or evaluation hints used by scorers. Table 6-1 summarizes the core fields.

Table 6-1. Core fields in an MLflow evaluation dataset

The expectations field deserves special attention. It is optional, but it is often what makes the dataset useful. The expectations field can hold a reference answer, a list of required facts, retrieval targets, or natural-language instructions for a judge. In practice, this means you do not need a single rigid definition of “ground truth.” For some test cases, a full expected response is appropriate. For others, especially open-ended support questions, it is better to specify the facts that must appear or the documents that should have been retrieved. Choose the lightest structure that still lets you evaluate the behavior you care about.

MLflow also stores system fields such as creation time, last update time, creator, and source. These fields are not part of the test case itself, but they help you track where the dataset came from, how it changed, and which version was used in a given evaluation run. That lineage becomes important once multiple people contribute examples or when you need to compare results across iterations.

In the next section, we will build an evaluation dataset for Unity Airways using examples drawn from traces and curated test cases and then register it so it can be reused across evaluation runs.

How to Build an Evaluation Dataset

A good evaluation expectations field dataset captures how users actually interact with your system. For the Unity Airways agent, that means examples covering real booking, refund, and policy questions that the agent might receive. You can build such evaluation datasets from three main avenues:

Existing traces

Use production or development traces already captured through MLflow Tracing. This method anchors your evaluation in authentic user interactions and helps you detect regressions that affect real-world behavior.

Domain expert labels

Import annotations or feedback collected through MLflow Labeling Sessions, which will be discussed in detail later in this chapter. These human-labeled examples provide accurate references and serve as the gold standard for testing factual correctness and groundedness.

Curated examples

Create a diverse set of test cases manually. These cases should cover edge scenarios that may not appear frequently in live data, such as rare fare classes, overlapping waivers, or complex itinerary changes. This dataset must evolve as your application is used by end users.

Together, these sources produce a balanced, realistic dataset for consistent and reproducible evaluation in MLflow 3.x.

To make this process easier, MLflow 3.x includes a dedicated evaluation dataset SDK, available under mlflow.genai.datasets. This SDK allows you to create, manage, and version datasets directly from code. It replaces manual CSV file handling with governed, versioned assets in Unity Catalog. Each dataset is automatically versioned, ensuring complete lineage between data, scorers, and evaluation runs. You can create new datasets, append or update records, and retrieve prior versions through simple API calls. Some of the most commonly used methods include:

create_dataset()

Creates a new evaluation dataset and stores it under a specified name or path.

get_dataset()

Retrieves an existing dataset for reading, updating, or reuse.

delete_dataset()

Deletes a dataset that is no longer needed while preserving lineage in MLflow.

With these methods, evaluation datasets become first-class MLflow objects that are automatically versioned and traceable to experiments and models. We will now explore how to leverage these Fluent APIs for the creation and management of such datasets.

Create a dataset

The first step is to create an MLflow-managed evaluation dataset. You could store test cases in a regular Unity Catalog table, but creating the dataset through MLflow gives you the abstraction that the rest of the evaluation workflow expects: a named evaluation dataset that you can load with get_dataset(); update with merge_records(); and tag, search, and populate directly from traces. MLflow’s dataset APIs and UI are built around that object, which is why we create it here instead of starting with a plain table: 

import mlflow
from mlflow.genai.datasets import create_dataset

# Create a managed evaluation dataset
first_dataset = create_dataset(
    name=f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.my_first_dataset",
)
print(f"Created evaluation dataset: {first_dataset.name}")

Once created, the dataset becomes the container for your evaluation records. In the next steps, you will add more examples, and MLflow will let you retrieve and update the dataset through the same interface over time.

Add records to the dataset

There are several approaches we can follow to add records to the dataset that we have just created.

Approach 1: Using existing traces

One of the best ways to create a realistic dataset is to use MLflow traces captured from the Unity Airways assistant. Each trace represents a real user query, model response, and associated context. You can use mlflow.search_traces() to retrieve recent production traces and add them to your dataset:

# Retrieve traces from previous experiment
traces = mlflow.search_traces(
    experiment_ids=EXPERIMENT_IDS,
    filter_string=("traces.status = 'OK'"),
    order_by=["attributes.timestamp_ms DESC"],
    max_results=10
)
print(f"Found {len(traces)} successful traces")

# Transform traces into the format expected by merge_records
records = [
    {
        "inputs": {"question": row["request"]["messages"][0]["content"]},
    }
    for _, row in traces.iterrows()
]

# Add the traces to the evaluation dataset
first_dataset = first_dataset.merge_records(records)
print(f"Added {len(records)} records to evaluation dataset")

This method builds a dataset rooted in actual user interactions, ensuring that your evaluation reflects live behavior. This dataset now acts as a managed table with lineage and metadata tracked automatically.

Approach 2: Using domain expert labels

You can also incorporate expert feedback collected through MLflow Labeling Sessions. For example, Unity Airways policy specialists might label agent responses for accuracy or completeness. You can also search for expert feedback using get_labeling_sessions(). These labels can be synced directly into an evaluation dataset, as follows:

# Using domain expert labels
import mlflow.genai.labeling as labeling

# Retrieve available labeling sessions
sessions = labeling.get_labeling_sessions()
for s in sessions:
    print(f"Session: {s.name}  (ID: {s.labeling_session_id})")

# Sync the first labeling session into the evaluation dataset
sessions[0].sync(to_dataset=f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.my_first_dataset")
print("Synchronized expert labels into evaluation dataset.")

This approach combines expert-validated ground truth with historical traces and adds reference answers to your dataset. Later in this chapter, we will look more closely at different ways of collecting human feedback to create an evaluation dataset.

Approach 3: Using curated examples

Curated data can help broaden coverage and explore unusual or risky queries. You can define evaluation examples manually in code. Each record should follow the evaluation schema, containing inputs and optional expectations and other metadata fields, like so:

# Using curated examples
curated_examples = [
    {
        "inputs": {
            "question": "Can I refund a partially used ticket for a delayed flight?"
        },
        "expectations": {
            "expected_response": "Refund depends on fare type and delay duration."
        },
    {
        "inputs": {"question": "Can I change my Lite ticket for tomorrow?"},
        "expectations": {"expected_response": "Lite tickets cannot be changed after 24 
            hours of purchase."}
    },
    {
        "inputs": {"question": "Refund for a canceled flight with waiver code WX-2025?"},
        "expectations": {"expected_response": "Refund permitted if the waiver code is valid 
            for the affected segment."}
    }
]
first_dataset = first_dataset.merge_records(curated_examples)

You can also import existing datasets, either as a list of dictionaries or as a Pandas DataFrame. These can then be merged with an existing MLflow evaluation dataset or used to create a new one. The next example demonstrates how to create a new dataset from data imported from a Unity Catalog table:

# Read 50 samples from Unity Airways QA dataset in Unity Catalog
eval_data_df = spark.read.table(
    f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.qa_dataset"
).limit(50)
display(eval_data_df)

Executing this code segment will display the eval_data_df, as Figure 6-4 shows.

Now we can use the imported dataset to create a new evaluation dataset as follows:

# Create an evaluation dataset
eval_dataset_new = create_dataset(
    name=f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.eval_dataset",
)
print(f"Created evaluation dataset: {eval_dataset_new.name}")

# Transform columns to match evaluation dataset schema
imported_data = eval_data_df.selectExpr(
    "struct(Question as question) as inputs",
    "struct(Answer as expected_response) as expectations"
)
# Update the dataset with imported cases
eval_dataset_new = eval_dataset_new.merge_records(imported_data)

This code segment shows how to create a new dataset using the imported data. Likewise, imported data can update an existing dataset through the merge_records() function, like so:

first_dataset = first_dataset.merge_records(imported_data)

Update or extend existing datasets

Evaluation datasets are versioned automatically. When you add or modify records, MLflow creates a new dataset version while preserving lineage. You can update datasets using get_dataset() and merge_records():

from mlflow.genai.datasets import get_dataset

# Load an existing dataset
eval_dataset_imported = get_dataset(
    name=f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.eval_dataset"
)

eval_dataset_imported = eval_dataset_imported.merge_records(curated_examples)
print("Updated the imported dataset with curated examples.")

Delete older datasets

You can remove outdated datasets while MLflow keeps the run lineage intact. Past runs still record the dataset’s name and version (for example, …@v7) and remain reproducible from their logged artifacts. If the dataset is soft-deleted or archived, you can still resolve that version; after a hard purge, the lineage reference remains visible on the run but cannot be resolved back to the table. For long-term reproducibility, it’s best to archive or attach a snapshot of the evaluation rows as a run artifact before deletion:

from mlflow.genai.datasets import delete_dataset
# Delete an existing dataset
delete_dataset(
    name=f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.my_first_dataset"
)
print("Deleted the old dataset.")
Warning

The evaluation dataset SDK, while simplifying dataset management, is currently subject to several practical limitations. Each dataset is restricted to a maximum of 2,000 records, and each entry supports no more than 20 expectation fields. Particularly large datasets may necessitate partitioning across multiple tables or schemas. For updated limitations and feature availability, refer to the MLflow documentation on GenAI evaluation datasets.

The dataset that we created in this section will be used in all evaluation runs in the following sections. With this dataset in place, you can proceed to define scorers that assess dimensions such as groundedness, factual accuracy, and coherence of the responses.

Designing and Managing Scorers

A scorer is a specialized function or component that evaluates the raw prediction (often text) from a GenAI application and transforms it into measurable, actionable metrics, effectively turning a prediction into something a team can quantify and trust. A response is just text until a scorer says “this is relevant,” “that is unsafe,” or “please add the phone number.” In MLflow 3.x, scorers do exactly that: they transform raw predictions into measurable metrics. This section shows how to design those scorers and register them for reuse in either offline evaluations or live production monitoring.

What Makes a Good Scorer

A good scorer is boring in the best possible way: predictable, explainable, and directly tied to outcomes you care about. The goal is to make a reliable and reusable instrument that accurately measures quality when traffic spikes, prompts drift, or product managers change the copy at the last minute.

Let’s review some principles to use when you design or accept a scorer.

Single point of truth

A scorer should measure one thing at a time. “Contains contact info” is one scorer. “Uses a professional tone” is another. Do not overload a scorer with a dozen checks. Clear scope makes monitoring dashboards readable and alerts actionable. When a red bar appears on a chart labeled contact_info_present, nobody needs a meeting to guess what went wrong.

Stable interface

Similar inputs should yield similar scores today and next month. You achieve this through determinism, resilience, and thresholds:

Determinism

For code-based scorers, avoid randomness. For LLM judges, fix prompts and temperature, and pin the model version, if your platform allows it.

Resilience

Normalize text before testing. Treat “1-800-UNITY-AIR” and “1800 Unity Air” as the same thing. When checking for dates, parse them rather than searching for a specific string.

Thresholds

Calibrate decision thresholds with labeled data so small wording changes don’t flip outcomes. For example, label 100 past answers as Helpful or Unhelpful and plot word counts. Assume that Helpful falls between 40–110 words; Unhelpful cluster <25 or >140. Set Pass = 40–110, Review band = 25–39 or 111–140, Fail = <25 or >140. Record these ranges with the scorer version and validate per slice (e.g., lite fares, multisegment itineraries).

Interpretable scale

Map results to a common scale, such as 0.0 to 1.0. A simple interpretation guideline helps the team work faster. For example, “0.9 means production ready for this dimension” or “0.5 means caution.” If the scorer is discrete, document what each bucket means.

Deterministic first, judgment second

If something can be checked with code, do it. Save LLM judges for what truly needs human-like interpretation. Deterministic logic is cheaper, faster, and easier to explain. LLM judges are powerful for relevance, safety, and nuanced correctness, but they should not replace a simple regular expression for a phone number.

Grounded in the use case

Tie every scorer to a real outcome. If customers need clear refund steps, prioritize response completeness over average token count. Use a simple test: if a drop in this score would change what the system does, keep it; if not, rethink it or demote it to a debug-only metric.

Economical at scale

Design with latency and cost in mind. Code-based scorers can run on every request. LLM judges might run at a sample rate in production. Support sampling knobs and offline evaluation. Think about budgets the same way you think about rate limits.

Version and register

Treat scorers like code artifacts. Name them, version them, and register them so that offline evaluations and online monitors reuse the exact same logic. You should be able to say, “This chart was produced by response_coherence scorer version 3.”

Portable and reusable

Ensure the same scorer definition works in development notebooks, in scheduled jobs, and in online monitoring services that attach feedback to traces. Avoid any environment-specific assumptions.

Ask three questions before you design any scorer: does it matter, does it behave, and can we explain it. If the answer to all three is yes and the scorer is versioned, lightweight to run, and sharply focused on one objective, you can rely on its numbers in dashboards, quality gates, and postmortems with confidence rather than doubt.

Now that the principles are clear, we will move from ideas to practice and build scorers that turn those ideas into measurable signals.

Code-Based Scorers

Code-based scorers are lightweight Python functions that convert deterministic checks into numeric scores or booleans with concise rationales. They run locally, incur no token cost, and are reproducible, which makes them ideal for continuous evaluations and regression tests. Implement them as ordinary functions decorated with @scorer that return a Feedback value, giving you full control to inspect any part of the trace. Typical uses include latency and token measurements, exact matching, schema validation, presence checks for phone numbers or dates, verification of flight code formats, and enforcement of business rules such as price limits, fare class consistency, or refund eligibility. The same definitions work in both offline evaluations and live production monitoring.

Let’s now implement a simple but useful code-based scorer: response length. Very short answers are often unhelpful. Very long ones waste the reader’s time and increase token costs. Here is an example that implements an ideal response length threshold:

from mlflow.genai.scorers import scorer
from mlflow.entities import Feedback

@scorer(name="response_length")
def ua_response_length_scorer(outputs) -> Feedback:
    response = outputs if isinstance(outputs, str) else outputs.get('response') or 
        outputs.get('outputs', {}).get('response', '')
    word_count = len(str(response).split())

    if word_count < 5:
        return Feedback(value=0.0, rationale=f"Response too short ({word_count} words)")
    elif word_count > 120:
        return Feedback(value=0.5, rationale=f"Response quite long ({word_count} words)")
    else:
        return Feedback(value=1.0, rationale=f"Appropriate length ({word_count} words)")

This returns a numeric score and a text rationale that will be visible in MLflow. For example:

  • Input:

    {"response": "Yes."}

    Feedback:

    value=0.0, rationale: "Response too short (1 words)"

  • Input:

    {"response": "You can change within 24 hours; after that a fee applies based 
on fare class. Use Manage Booking or contact support to confirm fees before 
proceeding."}

    Feedback:

    value=1.0, rationale: "Appropriate length (36 words)"

The exact response length cutoffs are based on your call. Treat them like product decisions and calibrate on real traffic. Similarly, code-based scorers can be used to provide operational insight by calculating latency and token counts. If your tracing captures timing and token metadata, a deterministic scorer can report a normalized value that feeds service level objective (SLO) dashboards.

LLM Judges

LLM judges, also known as LLM-as-a-judge or LLM-based scorers, use LLMs to evaluate nuanced qualities such as relevance, safety, and correctness. They complement deterministic, code-based checks by adding human-like interpretation where rigid rules reach their limits. Each judge reads the full trace, including the request, any retrieved context, and the assistant’s response, and then returns a numeric score with a concise rationale. In MLflow 3.x these scorers operate in both offline evaluations and live production monitoring, and they attach Feedback entries to traces so teams can trend and investigate qualitative performance over time.

An LLM judge becomes appropriate when evaluation requires understanding or reasoning beyond simple pattern matching. Typical use cases include quality assessments that involve correctness, coherence, relevance, helpfulness, and adherence to instructions. Safety evaluations also benefit from LLM judges, such as detecting harmful or biased content, exposure of personal data, or violations of company and regulatory policies. LLM judges further help in complex scenarios that involve multiturn reasoning, multidocument synthesis, or responses that depend on context across modalities. In short, if your assessment hinges on meaning, intent, or subtlety rather than surface patterns, an LLM judge provides the right instrument.

Managed MLflow on Databricks supports two broad categories of LLM judges: built-in LLM judges and custom LLM judges.

Built-in LLM judges

Built-in judges provide preconfigured evaluations for common dimensions and return a Feedback object that can be logged, charted, and alerted on. These judges parse the trace, call an LLM using the configured model provider, and produce both a score and a rationale. Commonly used built-in judges include:

RelevanceToQuery

This judge evaluates whether the assistant’s reply directly addresses the user’s request. In the Unity Airways tool-calling agent, it can be used to confirm that a refund question receives a refund-focused answer rather than an explanation about baggage allowances.

Safety

This judge checks that the response avoids toxic or harmful content and does not disclose sensitive information. In the Unity Airways scenario, it validates that messages about flight disruptions remain calm, noninflammatory, and free of PII.

Correctness

This judge compares the response against ground truth or labeled answers to determine factual accuracy. In the Unity Airways scenario, it verifies that the stated cancellation window and fees match the airline’s verified policy text in the answer key.

RetrievalGroundedness

This judge assesses whether the answer is supported by retrieved context rather than speculation. In the Unity Airways scenario, it confirms that a fare-change explanation cites the specific fare rules pulled from the policy documents retrieved from Vector Search.

RetrievalRelevance

This judge evaluates whether the retrieved documents match the user’s request. In the Unity Airways scenario, it ensures that a missed-connection query retrieves connection and rebooking policy documents from Vector Search instead of lounge access details.

RetrievalSufficiency

This judge determines whether the retrieved set contains all information required to answer the question. In the Unity Airways scenario, it checks that both refund eligibility and processing time documentation are retrieved from Vector Search when the user asks how to obtain a refund and how long it will take.

The following snippet shows how multiple built-in judges can be imported for later evaluations that may be performed by the Unity Airways assistant:

from mlflow.genai.scorers import (
    RelevanceToQuery,
    Safety,
    RetrievalGroundedness,
    Correctness,
)

By default, the judges use Databricks-hosted LLMs that are designed for GenAI quality assessments. The model can be overridden per judge by passing a model argument that references a supported provider and model. Pinning models to the scorers helps to improve stability across runs. Here are some examples:

eval_model = "databricks:/databricks-gpt-oss-120b"
ua_relevancy_scorer = RelevanceToQuery(model=eval_model)
ua_safety_scorer = Safety(model=eval_model)
ua_groundedness_scorer = RetrievalGroundedness(model=eval_model)
ua_correctness_scorer = Correctness(model=eval_model)

Custom LLM judges

Custom LLM judges address needs that go beyond the built-in judges and allow alignment with domain expert judgment. They become practical when applications grow in complexity and the evaluation criteria must match specific business requirements. MLflow provides several ways to define such judges, including a guidelines-based approach and a custom-prompt approach.

Guidelines judges

Guidelines judges let domain experts express rules as plain language. This approach works well for compliance, style, or must-include content. MLflow offers the following guidelines-based judges:

Guidelines

This judge tests the response against global “pass” or “fail” criteria such as tone, brand mentions, or required disclaimers. In the Unity Airways scenario, it can be used to enforce a professional tone, a reference to “Unity Airways,” and the standard note that processes vary by fare class.

ExpectationsGuidelines

This judge applies per-example rules supplied as Expectations in the dataset to judge compliance for that specific case. In the Unity Airways scenario, it requires the phone number for high-value bookings or mandates a link to the rebooking portal for disruption cases specified in the row’s expectations.

Guidelines-based judges use a fine-tuned LLM to determine whether text meets your specified criteria. The judge receives a context payload, such as a JSON dictionary containing fields like request, response, user_preferences, or retrieved_​docu⁠ments, and you can reference these keys directly in your written guidelines. It then applies your natural-language rules to define “pass” or “fail” conditions and produces a binary verdict together with a detailed rationale. If you need to, you can change the underlying model by providing a model argument in the judge definition, similarly to built-in LLM judges. Figure 6-5 illustrates this process.

Let’s return to our Unity Airways assistant. Assume that we want to evaluate whether the Unity Airways assistant responds in a professional tone and completely addresses the customer’s question. The following examples show how such criteria translate into machine-enforceable checks using the Guidelines class judges:

from mlflow.genai.scorers import Guidelines

ua_professional_tone_scorer = Guidelines(
    name="professional_tone",
    guidelines="""
    The response must use professional, courteous language appropriate for airline 
    customer service.

    Requirements:
    - Use polite and respectful language
    - Avoid casual expressions or slang
    - Maintain a helpful and solution-oriented tone
    - Include appropriate greetings or closings when relevant
    """,
    model=eval_model,
)
ua_completeness_scorer = Guidelines(
    name="response_completeness", 
    guidelines="""
    The response must completely address the customer's question:
    - Directly answer the specific question asked
    - Provide all relevant details mentioned in the expected response
    - Include next steps or additional resources when appropriate
    - Avoid generic responses when specific information is requested
    """,
    model=eval_model,
)

Custom judges

Some situations call for full control over the judging prompt and the need to return more granular outputs than a simple “pass” or “fail.” An example includes categorizing an answer as “great,” “ok,” or “bad,” and then mapping that label to an ordinal score. MLflow provides an API that accepts a prompt template and a choice set to implement this pattern:

from mlflow.genai.judges import make_judge
from typing import Literal

ua_coherence_scorer = make_judge(
    name="coherence",
    instructions=(
       "Evaluate if the response is coherent, maintaining a constant tone, and following 
           airline policies"
       "Question: {{ inputs }}\n"
       "Response: {{ outputs }}\n"
       "Categorize the response as 'coherent', 'somewhat coherent', or 'incoherent'."
   ),
)

This pattern separates concerns in a way that remains explainable to stakeholders. The judge determines a categorical verdict and records reasoning. Using the coherence judge, the scorer reads both the question and the reply and returns a categorical verdict plus a numeric score. For example:

  • Input:

    {"question": "My flight was downgraded from Business to Economy. What compensation do 
I get on an EU route?",
"response": "We are sorry about the change. EU rules require compensation based on 
distance. You can choose cash or a voucher. Use the claims portal to submit your 
request."}

    Feedback:

    value = "coherent", rationale = "The response stays on topic, 
           follows policy, and gives a clear next step."

This pattern turns subjective qualities into measurable signals that you can track, compare, and use to make confident release decisions.

Warning

The make_judge API requires MLflow >= 3.4.0. For earlier versions, use the deprecated custom_prompt_judge instead.

Scorer Lifecycle Management

You can reuse the same scorer in development notebooks and live production monitoring. Scorer lifecycle management ensures consistency, traceability, and reliability across both offline evaluation and live production monitoring. By governing how scorers are registered, versioned, and activated, teams can reuse the same evaluation logic that validated a model in preproduction to continuously assess its quality in active production. This alignment eliminates metric drift, supports reproducible comparisons across model versions, and enables trustworthy performance tracking over time. It also simplifies governance by ensuring every quality signal comes from a standardized and auditable scorer definition, whether from batch tests or live traces.

Scorer lifecycle management API

To reuse the very same logic in different stages, each scorer can be registered and managed through the scorer lifecycle API. Registration publishes the scorer so that services can look it up by name, apply it to live traces, and record feedback at a chosen sampling rate. After registration, production code can start, tune, pause, or retire scoring without changing the application’s core request path.

MLflow scorers support a set of instance methods expressed as regular function calls:

register()

This method publishes the scorer in the registry and returns a server-registered handle.

start()

This method enables online scoring with an optional sample_rate so expensive judges can run on a fraction of traffic.

update()

This method modifies the configuration over time, which is useful during rollouts or incident triage.

stop()

This method disables online scoring for that scorer.

delete()

This removes the scorer from the registry when it is no longer needed.

For example, we can register our scorers for later use as follows:

# Register built-in LLM judges
ua_relevancy_scorer.register()
ua_safety_scorer.register()
ua_groundedness_scorer.register()
ua_correctness_scorer.register()

# Register custom LLM judges
ua_professional_tone_scorer.register()
ua_completeness_scorer.register()
ua_coherence_scorer.register()

# Register code-based scorers
ua_response_length_scorer.register()

MLflow also exposes a set of registry functions under mlflow.genai.scorers to discover and manage scorers centrally. You can list available scorers, fetch one by name, or delete it using list_scorers(), get_scorer(), and delete_scorer(), respectively.

In practice, teams register all production-relevant scorers, pin model references for LLM judges, and document a short playbook for each scorer’s intended use. This approach ensures that the checks used in offline evaluation are the same ones enforcing quality in production, which simplifies comparisons over time and makes dashboards and alerts easier to trust.

Documentation and operator playbook

It is important to treat each scorer as a reusable instrument by providing a short description, examples of rationales, and a clear operator action so that a red bar on a dashboard translates into a concrete next step. Examples of descriptions include:

ua_response_length_scorer

This verifies that answers fall within a practical range, such as 5 to 120 words, which balances helpfulness with brevity. Typical rationales read like “Too short: 3 words” or “Appropriate length: 84 words.”

Action: When this score trends down, operators should sample recent conversations to see whether prompts have become overly terse or whether the assistant is refusing too often, then adjust prompts or refusal policies accordingly.

ua_professional_tone_scorer

This evaluates whether the assistant’s reply uses professional, courteous language appropriate for airline customer service and meets the stated requirements: polite and respectful wording, avoidance of slang, a helpful and solution-oriented tone, and appropriate greetings or closings when relevant. Typical rationales include “Polite and empathetic greeting with clear next steps,” “Content helpful but uses casual slang,” or “Direct answer but tone sounds abrupt and unsympathetic.”

Action: When this score declines, operators should review recent responses for shifts in tone, check prompt templates and style guides for accidental edits, and sample conversations where customers express frustration to ensure empathy and clarity are present. If needed, update a few-shot examples, add a tone reminder to the system prompt, or introduce a post-processor that adds brief, empathetic closings for sensitive scenarios.

With a concise playbook in place for what each score means and how to respond, the next step is to see these scorers in action.

Running and Comparing Evaluations in MLflow

An evaluation run is an MLflow run that organizes and stores the results of evaluating your GenAI application. Each evaluation run contains the same four components:

Traces

One trace for each input example in your evaluation dataset. A trace captures request and response content, intermediate steps, retrievals, timing, token counts, and tool calls where applicable.

Feedback

Quality assessments generated by your scorers. These may be LLM-based judgments, code-based checks, or hybrid signals that attach to each trace.

Metrics

Aggregate statistics computed from per-trace feedback, such as pass rates, averages, and distributions.

Metadata

Configuration that explains exactly how the evaluation executed: dataset name and version, model or agent version, prompt template identifiers, scorer definitions and versions, and environment details.

MLflow 3.x provides a unified API for running these evaluations through mlflow.genai.evaluate(). It logs results with lineage that links back to datasets, model versions, and trace identifiers. This makes root cause analysis and regression detection far more reliable than ad hoc notebooks or sticky notes with cryptic numbers.

Evaluation Run Structure

It helps to picture the run as a directory tree. The exact artifact layout can vary by project, but the structure illustrated in Figure 6-6 captures the spirit of what you will find.

This structured layout ensures that all necessary information—from the overall run context to individual traces and aggregate performance metrics—is readily accessible for analysis and comparison across different evaluation runs.

Note

In MLflow 3.x, mlflow.genai.evaluate() scores the trace, which includes the request, retrieved documents, tool calls, intermediate steps, the final output, timings, and token counts. Groundedness and retrieval relevance need the retrieved context. Safety and guidelines checks use the response together with metadata. Latency and cost come from span timings and tokens. In direct mode, MLflow creates a fresh trace via predict_fn. In answer-sheet mode, you provide existing traces. Evaluations judge the execution, not a standalone string.

Evaluating the Unity Airways Assistant

Let’s evaluate the Unity Airways tool-calling agent in this section. The application integrates retrieval, policy reasoning, and conversational response generation. A post-processor formats the final answer with citations. In Chapter 4, we registered this agent into Unity Catalog. That registration now pays off because we can load and evaluate it directly using MLflow 3.x, with clear model lineage and access controls.

Load the registered model, dataset, and scorers

Before running a full evaluation, we can perform a quick local check to confirm that the registered agent loads correctly and responds to a sample input. The following snippet uses mlflow.langchain.load_model() and ModelConfig to supply a development configuration. ModelConfig reads a YAML configuration file or a dictionary that mirrors the configuration used during registration, which ensures consistency between your development testing and the production environment without introducing changes to production settings:

import mlflow

# Define version and model location
model_uri = f"models:/{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.tool_calling_agent/{MODEL_VERSION}"

# Load the LangChain model from Unity Catalog and test
loaded_agent = mlflow.langchain.load_model(model_uri)
response = loaded_agent.invoke({'messages': [{'content': 'How do I book flights with 
    Unity Airways?',
   'role': 'user'}]})
print(response)

In this case, we retrieve an input example, which is stored in the ModelConfig, and then invoke the agent using this example. Figure 6-7 illustrates the MLflow Trace UI, which displays the execution trace of our agent for the provided input example.

This quick check ensures that the agent is correctly registered, dependencies are in place, and the model can produce valid responses before you begin evaluation. The output will contain a natural-language answer along with one or more policy citations, depending on the query.

Next, we can load our evaluation dataset prepared in the previous section of this chapter as follows:

from mlflow.genai.datasets import get_dataset

# Load the evaluation dataset
eval_dataset = get_dataset(
    name=f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.eval_dataset"
)

Finally, we can fetch our predefined scorers from scorer registry and assemble them into a single list, like so:

from mlflow.genai.scorers import get_scorer

# Load scorers
ua_relevancy_scorer = get_scorer(name="relevance_to_query")
ua_safety_scorer = get_scorer(name="safety")
ua_groundedness_scorer = get_scorer(name="retrieval_groundedness")
ua_correctness_scorer = get_scorer(name="correctness")
ua_professional_tone_scorer = get_scorer(name="professional_tone")
ua_completeness_scorer = get_scorer(name="response_completeness")
ua_coherence_scorer = get_scorer(name="coherence")
ua_response_length_scorer = get_scorer(name="response_length")

# Assemble scorers into a list
unity_airways_scorers = [
   ua_relevancy_scorer,
   ua_safety_scorer,
   ua_groundedness_scorer,
   ua_correctness_scorer,
   ua_professional_tone_scorer,
   ua_completeness_scorer,
   ua_coherence_scorer,
   ua_response_length_scorer
]

Now we have our agent, evaluation dataset, and scorers loaded and ready to be used in the MLflow evaluation run. The only additional ingredient we need is a prediction function that takes the dataset row as input and returns an agent response.

Prepare the predict_fn() function

MLflow’s GenAI evaluation entry point expects a predict_fn() when using direct evaluation mode or answer-sheet evaluation mode. We use predict_fn() here to test the live agent. A minimal predict_fn() for the Unity Airways assistant could be as follows:

from typing import Dict

# Wraps the Unity Airways agent so that mlflow.genai.evaluate can call it.
def agent_predict_fn(question: str) -> Dict[str, str]:
    return loaded_agent.invoke({
        "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": question}
        ]
    })

If your agent expects a richer input dictionary, adapt the function to extract fields from the row. Make sure the schema you pass to evaluation matches what the agent expects. It might sound obvious, yet this mismatch is one of the top causes of empty result sets.

Running an evaluation

By now, we have successfully loaded all the required components into our environment: the agent, the evaluation dataset, and the scorers. Now, we can initiate the MLflow run, which will handle the heavy lifting, by executing the following code:

import mlflow
# Run evaluation with predefined scorers
with mlflow.start_run(run_name=f"ua_rag_eval_baseline"):
    mlflow.set_tag("model_version", MODEL_VERSION)
    mlflow.set_tag("dataset_version", "eval_dataset")
    eval_results = mlflow.genai.evaluate(
        data=eval_dataset,
        predict_fn=agent_predict_fn,
        scorers=unity_airways_scorers
    )

When the cell finishes, MLflow has produced a new evaluation run that includes traces, per-row feedback, and aggregate metrics. When executed on a Databricks notebook, the MLflow UI, displaying the evaluation run details, is automatically embedded below the code cell. You can also access the run in the full MLflow UI to view a leaderboard of metrics (Figure 6-8), examine a specific row’s trace, and download artifacts for later analysis if required. This consistent logging and lineage handling by MLflow ensures the same evaluation pattern works seamlessly across both development and production workflows.

By clicking on any selected trace, you can view more details about the trace and attached scores (Figure 6-9).

Comparing Evaluation Runs

Running one evaluation is helpful. Running several against the same dataset is where insight appears. The fundamental rule for making meaningful comparisons is to maintain a fixed dataset version and pin the model or agent version, altering only one variable per run. If two variables must be changed simultaneously, ensure both are explicitly tagged and the reason for the dual change is clearly documented.

Naming and tagging runs for comparison

When naming and tagging runs, ensure they reflect the specific hypothesis being tested. For example, here is a small pattern that produces two comparable runs, one with the LLM set at a lower temperature and one at a higher temperature:

# Create a variant predict function that uses lower temperature
def agent_predict_fn_temp_0p2(question: str):
    return loaded_agent.invoke({
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}],
        "temperature": temperature
    })
# Run evaluation 
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="ua_rag_eval_temp_0p2"):
    mlflow.set_tag("model_version", MODEL_VERSION)
    mlflow.set_tag("temperature", "0.2")
    res_0p2 = mlflow.genai.evaluate(
        data=eval_dataset,
        predict_fn=agent_predict_fn_temp_0p2,  
        scorers=unity_airways_scorers
    )

# Create a variant predict function that uses high temperature
def agent_predict_fn_temp_0p6(question: str):
    return loaded_agent.invoke({
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}],
        "temperature": temperature
    })
# Run evaluation 
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="ua_rag_eval_temp_0p6"):
    mlflow.set_tag("model_version", MODEL_VERSION)
    mlflow.set_tag("temperature", "0.6")
    res_0p6 = mlflow.genai.evaluate(
        data=eval_dataset,
        predict_fn=agent_predict_fn_temp_0p6,
        scorers=unity_airways_scorers
    )

In the MLflow UI, filter by the model_version tag and select both runs. Look at the headline metrics for groundedness, brand compliance, and response length. If pass rates move in opposite directions, open the traces that flipped. Those are your most informative examples.

In the MLflow UI, here’s what you do: filter your runs using the model_version tag and select the runs you want to examine. Now, take a close look at the main metrics such as response_completeness or RetrievalGroundedness (Figure 6-10). If you notice that the pass rates for these metrics are moving in opposite directions, you’ve found something interesting! Open the traces for those specific runs that showed a change. These examples are your goldmine for debugging and improving your GenAI application.

By clicking on any selected request in the view in Figure 6-10, you can view more details about aspects like the outputs of attached scores, model output, and expected output (Figure 6-11).

Beyond side-by-side comparison

After you are comfortable with the comparison techniques we just covered, you can layer on a few additional techniques to sharpen your judgments:

  • First, introduce difficulty bands by labeling examples as easy, medium, or hard, because gains on easy questions can hide regressions on hard ones.

  • Next, add confidence intervals for scalar scorers by computing bootstrap intervals so you can tell whether a difference is meaningful, and store these intervals as artifacts so they appear with the run.

  • Finally, maintain a small table of failure examples by persisting the failing traces from the previous run and checking them explicitly in the next run, which prevents yesterday’s bugs from slipping back in unnoticed.

Diagnosing Regressions and Troubleshooting with Traces

While aggregated numbers reveal when something is wrong, traces help to dig deeper to understand what is wrong. If a metric dips, such as a six-point drop in the professional tone scorer after a post-processor change, open several failing traces and look for patterns:

  • Check whether responses lost courteous greetings or empathetic phrasing, whether slang or abrupt wording slipped in, or whether helpful next steps disappeared.

  • Verify that citations still point to the correct policy documents, since off-topic references can pull the message off tone by forcing irrelevant context.

  • Confirm that formatting did not shorten replies below your minimum length, because overly brief answers often read as curt and unhelpful.

Because each feedback record attaches to a specific trace, you can quickly assemble a small set of reproducible examples for the developer or prompt author. If a change lifts one metric while hurting another, use these traces to judge whether the trade-off is acceptable or whether you should refine the scorer, adjust the prompt templates, or revert the post-processing step.

Traces also make routine troubleshooting faster:

  • If a run finishes with zero traces, check that the data argument matches what predict_fn() expects, confirm column names and types, and validate inputs first when your model has a strict signature.

  • If a scorer crashes for a subset of rows, wrap its logic defensively, return a neutral value with a clear explanation when inputs are missing, and log the exception as scorer feedback so you can filter and fix those rows later.

  • If outputs are inconsistent from one call to the next, normalize the agent’s output in a post-processor so scorers never have to guess whether they are receiving a dictionary or a string.

  • If performance is slow, inspect timing inside traces.

  • When retrieval dominates, review index health and context window size.

  • When judge calls dominate, try a smaller judge for canary checks and reserve a larger judge for release candidates.

In all cases, let the traces guide you. They capture the exact inputs, intermediate steps, and outputs that turned a high-level metric into a red number, and they point directly to the line of code or prompt token that needs attention. Use the checklist in Table 6-5 as a guide when troubleshooting your GenAI application.

Table 6-5. Trace-driven troubleshooting checklist
SymptomWhat to checkFast fix
Run finishes with zero tracesdata schema versus predict_fn expectations, column names, input typesValidate inputs early and align the schema with the function signature.
Scorer crashes on some rowsMissing fields or unexpected typesAdd defensive checks, return a neutral value with an explanation, log the exception as feedback.
Output shape varies by callSometimes a dict, sometimes a stringNormalize outputs in a post-processor so scorers receive a consistent structure.
Slow performanceSpan timings inside tracesIf retrieval dominates, check index health and context window size. If judge calls dominate, sample a smaller judge for canaries and reserve the larger judge for release candidates.

Even the best scorer suite does not capture every nuance. For example, airline policy questions can be subtle. Tone and empathy matter. Edge cases surprise everyone. The final step in a mature evaluation workflow is to bring human judgment into the loop, but to do it with structure so that human input becomes useful evaluation data, not folklore.

Multiturn Evaluation

In the earlier sections, evaluation focused primarily on single-turn interactions, where a user input is paired with a corresponding model response and assessed independently. However, real-world GenAI applications are more complex than this. Responses depend on prior turns, requiring the model to retain context, track user intent, and adapt as the conversation evolves. As a result, what is evaluated as good at the single-turn level does not guarantee that a conversation as a whole is successful. A GenAI application may produce locally relevant responses while still failing to complete the intended task, maintain consistency, or deliver a satisfying user experience.

In MLflow 3.10, multiturn evaluation was introduced to address this limitation by treating the entire conversation as the unit of analysis, enabling a more holistic assessment of system behavior. Rather than optimizing individual responses, it evaluates how effectively the system progresses toward a successful outcome across turns.

Preparing data for multiturn evaluation

To enable multiturn evaluation, we can group traces that belong to the same interaction using a shared session or conversation ID. MLflow uses this identifier to reconstruct the full dialogue, including the sequence of user messages, model responses, and any intermediate tool calls, so that evaluation can be performed over the conversation as a whole rather than on individual turns.

The way to do this is to add the session identifier as trace metadata when each turn is logged using the MLflow API:

mlflow.update_current_trace(metadata={"mlflow.trace.session": session_id})

MLflow also supports conversation simulation (ConversationSimulator), which is useful when real conversation data is limited. With ConversationSimulator, you define the conversation goals, personas, or behavioral guidelines, and MLflow generates synthetic multiturn conversations that can be evaluated just like real sessions. This makes it possible to build repeatable benchmarks and test edge cases before deployment:

import mlflow
from mlflow.genai.simulators import ConversationSimulator

# Unity Air Test Cases
test_cases = [
    {
        "goal": "Reschedule booking id xaji0y6dpbhsahxt, confirm the fare difference and 
            whether the LITE fare brand allows changes, and handle the expected rejection 
            gracefully",
        "persona": "A frequent business traveler who is direct and impatient, expects quick 
            answers, and pushes back if the agent is vague about costs or policies.",
    },
    {
        "goal": "Ask about the refund status for booking id xxc02dgtfgq5c34d. Verify that 
            the refund has been processed",
        "persona": "A non-technical traveler who speaks in casual language, sometimes  
            provides incomplete information, and needs the agent to ask clarifying 
            questions."
    },
]

# Conversation Simulator
simulator = ConversationSimulator(
    test_cases=test_cases,
    max_turns=5,
)

Multiturn judges and scorers

Once conversation traces are prepared, evaluation is carried out using multiturn scorers. Unlike single-turn judges, which evaluate each response independently, multiturn judges take into account temporal dependencies and whether the application is making meaningful progress toward a goal. Table 6-6 shows some examples of multiturn judges.

Table 6-6. List of built-in multiturn judges
Judge nameWhat it measures
ConversationCompleteness Does the agent address all user questions throughout the conversation?
ConversationalGuidelines Do the assistant’s responses comply with provided guidelines?
ConversationalRoleAdherence Does the assistant maintain its assigned role throughout the conversation?
ConversationalSafety Are the assistant’s responses safe and free of harmful content?
ConversationalToolCallEfficiency Was tool usage across the conversation efficient and appropriate?
KnowledgeRetention Does the assistant correctly retain information from earlier user inputs?
UserFrustration Is the user frustrated? Was the frustration resolved?

Besides built-in multiturn judges, we can also create custom multiturn scorers:

from mlflow.genai.judges import make_judge
from typing import Literal

professional_tone_judge = make_judge(
    name="professional_tone",
    instructions=(
        "Review this conversation:\n\n{{ conversation }}\n\n"
        "Evaluate whether the assistant maintained a professional, courteous, "
        "and airline-appropriate tone throughout the conversation. "
        "Consider: empathy when handling complaints, clear and polite language, "
        "and avoiding overly casual or robotic responses.\n\n"
        "Rate as 'professional' or 'unprofessional'."
    ),
    feedback_value_type=bool,
)

The {{ conversation }} variable injects the complete conversation history in a readable format for the judge to analyze.

We can then evaluate using both multiturn and single-turn judges:

results = mlflow.genai.evaluate(
    data=simulator,
    predict_fn=predict_fn,
    scorers=[
        ConversationCompleteness(),
        Safety(), # This is a single-turn judge
        professional_tone_judge
    ],
)

After running the evaluation, we can examine the results at the session level, as shown in Figure 6-12.

We can also look into individual turns to inspect the results from single-turn judges (safety) (Figure 6-13).

At first glance, it may seem that multiturn evaluation is the better choice, since it can cover both multiturn and single-turn scenarios. While this is true in principle, it doesn’t mean single-turn evaluation is irrelevant. For applications that are inherently stateless such as summarization or classification, where prior context does not affect output quality, single-turn evaluation remains the more appropriate choice. Cost and speed also matter. Multiturn evaluation involves longer context and multiple steps, which naturally increases execution time and evaluation cost compared to single-turn setups.

As a rule of thumb, use single-turn evaluation for fast, focused validation of stateless tasks, and reserve multiturn evaluation for scenarios where context and interaction history truly matter.

Capturing Human Feedback

A healthy GenAI application depends on human feedback. Automated scorers move fast and cover breadth, but they often miss nuance. Users notice tone. Reviewers spot subtle factual gaps. Domain experts demand industry-specific rigor. MLflow 3.x treats that human feedback as a first-class signal by letting you attach feedback directly to traces, store it in a structured way, and reuse it for evaluation, fine-tuning, or targeted debugging later. The result is a single loop that closes the distance between what your app did, what people thought of it, and what you should change next. In this section, we cover how the feedback model works and practical patterns for collecting it from developers, domain experts, and end users.

Data Model Overview

MLflow keeps human judgment close to the execution it describes. It stores that judgment as an Assessment object attached to an MLflow trace. A trace is the record of a single application execution, including request and response data plus the spans that capture intermediate steps. This matters because it lets you review an answer in context. Instead of labeling an output in isolation, you can inspect the full path that produced it.

For human-in-the-loop workflows, two assessment types matter most, Feedback and Expectations:

Feedback

Records how the application actually behaved. It can be a thumbs-up, a numeric score, a pass/fail label, or a short rationale from a reviewer, an end user, an LLM judge, or a code-based check.

Expectations

Record what the application should have produced for that input. It can hold a reference answer, required facts, structured output, or even the documentation that should have been retrieved. Both feedback and expectations can be attached either to the whole trace or to a specific span when you want to label a particular step such as retrieval.

As Figure 6-14 shows, MLflow also records the source of an Assessment. For Feedback, the source can identify a human reviewer, an LLM judge, or a code-based evaluator. Expectations are human-authored ground truth and carry source metadata as well. That distinction becomes useful once multiple signals start to accumulate. A supervisor’s review, a customer thumbs-down, and an automated judge score may all be valuable, but they do not mean the same thing and should not be treated as interchangeable.

This model is especially useful for RAG and agent systems. In the Unity Airways assistant, a single trace might carry an expectation for the canonical refund answer, feedback on tone and completeness, and a separate assessment on the retriever span if the wrong policy document was fetched. Because these assessments stay attached to the trace, you can later search traces by assessment fields, inputs, tags, and other attributes, then inspect the exact execution path behind the judgment.

Collecting Human Feedback

Human feedback can be grouped according to the product lifecycle stage and is typically collected from three different groups: developers who supply ongoing annotations during the build phase, domain experts who offer curated judgments, and end users in production who provide quick impressions such as thumbs up/down. The data model stays the same during all these stages. The collection workflow differs only in who clicks what and where the data lands.

Adding developer annotations

During development and staging, your team should read traces and leave targeted notes. This is where you catch regressions early and mark examples for later tests. In the MLflow UI, open the Logs tab, click a trace, select either the root Span or a child Span, and add an Assessment (Figure 6-15). Use a consistent naming scheme such as dev_accuracy_score or dev_needs_disclosure, and write specific rationales. After you add the first Assessment with a new name, a column with that name appears in the Logs tab, which makes bulk triage faster and more reliable.

For quick scoring experiments you can also log developer feedback through code. This approach helps you annotate many Trace objects in one pass after a notebook review session. Here is an example:

import mlflow
from typing import Optional
from mlflow.entities.assessment import AssessmentSource, AssessmentSourceType

def mark_dev_accuracy(trace_id: str, score: float, note: Optional[str], 
        dev_email: str) -> None:
    mlflow.log_feedback(
        trace_id=trace_id,
        name="dev_accuracy_score",
        value=score,
        rationale=note,
        source=AssessmentSource(
            source_type=AssessmentSourceType.HUMAN,
            source_id=dev_email,
        ),
    )

Developer feedback is often opinionated. Therefore, they should be treated as advisory unless a designated reviewer signs off.

Sending traces for domain-expert feedback

Some answers require expert judgment. For example, flight fare refund eligibility is often entangled with fare families, code-share flights, and local consumer protections. In these cases you want a customer support supervisor or a policy owner to determine what is correct and to write the canonical response. MLflow Labeling Sessions provide a structured way to do this. A session is a curated queue of Trace objects to review using predefined label schemas. Each session is also an MLflow run, which allows you to search, audit, and track outcomes over time.

We can start by defining exactly what we want experts to supply. For Unity Airways, the typical schema includes a categorical accuracy rating and an ideal response text that contains the mandatory disclosures.

import mlflow
from mlflow.genai.label_schemas import create_label_schema, InputCategorical, InputText
from mlflow.genai.labeling import create_labeling_session

# Define expert labels
accuracy_schema = create_label_schema(
    name="response_accuracy",
    type="feedback",
    title="Is the response factually accurate?",
    input=InputCategorical(options=["Accurate", "Partially Accurate", "Inaccurate"]),
    overwrite=True,
)

ideal_schema = create_label_schema(
    name="expected_response",
    type="expectation",
    title="What would be the ideal response?",
    input=InputText(),
    overwrite=True,
)

# Create a labeling session and add candidate traces
session = create_labeling_session(
    name="refund_policy_review",
    label_schemas=[accuracy_schema.name, ideal_schema.name],
)

# Select traces to review. Example: the most recent 20 with a thumbs-down.
traces = mlflow.search_traces(
    filter_string="assessments.user_feedback = false",
    max_results=20
)
session.add_traces(traces)
print("Share with experts:", session.url)  # Review App link for domain experts

When experts open the Review App link, they can view the original user question and the agent response and read any existing end-user or developer feedback. They then record their judgments by selecting a categorical accuracy rating and by providing the canonical expected response with required disclosures. MLflow stores these entries as Assessments on the underlying traces, which preserves full context for later analysis.

Note

The Review App Chat UI requires an agent deployed to a model serving endpoint. We will discuss the Review App in detail in the section “Deploying to Databricks Model Serving,” in Chapter 8. Figure 8-7 shows a Databricks Review App Chat UI.

Collecting end-user feedback

In production, you should collect signals with as little friction as possible. Most users will not write essays. They will click a simple icon and, if prompted, add a short note. This is perfectly acceptable. High volumes of lightweight signals reveal hot spots, confusing moments, and tone mismatches. In the Unity Airways assistant, each assistant reply displays thumbs-up and thumbs-down controls with an optional text box. We will discuss collecting end-user feedback with code samples in Chapter 9 within the context of online monitoring.

Aligning LLM Judges with Human Feedback

We explored how to use LLM judges as a fast, scalable approach for evaluating GenAI applications and enabling rapid iteration. While these judges provide a strong foundation, they do not always reflect how people within an organization perceive quality. For instance, an LLM judge might rate a response as polite, whereas a human reviewer may disagree.

This misalignment can lead to misleading evaluation signals: an application may appear to perform well according to automated metrics yet still fall short of real user expectations. As a result, teams risk optimizing for metrics that fail to meaningfully correlate with user satisfaction or business outcomes.

MLflow addresses this by enabling the alignment of LLM judges with human feedback. At a high level, alignment involves teaching the judge to approximate human evaluation behavior using labeled examples. This process typically begins with collecting human feedback on a representative set of traces, where annotators provide both structured scores (e.g., good versus bad) and natural-language rationales explaining their decisions.

With the feedback collected, we can use MLflow built-in optimizers such as SIMBA and MemAlign to improve the judges. A detailed explanation of these optimizers is beyond the scope of this book, but the main idea is that these optimizers help the judge better reflect how humans evaluate quality without retraining the underlying model. For example, the MemAlign optimizer does this by giving the judge access to past human feedback, including both general guidelines and specific examples. As more feedback is collected, the judge can improve over time while remaining efficient and easy to update.

Once the optimization is completed, we need a way to validate that the judges have indeed improved. This can be done by comparing the judges’ scores with human evaluations on unseen traces, ensuring that any gains generalize beyond the traces used during optimization. Moreover, we can also inspect for qualitative improvements, such as better identification of edge cases or more consistent reasoning across similar scenarios. Figure 6-16 summarizes the overall process.

Conclusion and Key Takeaways

Evaluation for GenAI is an operating discipline. In this chapter, you learned how to turn real user questions into versioned evaluation datasets, define scorers for the behaviors that matter, and run evaluations that tie every result back to the exact traces, prompts, and code behind it. You also saw how human feedback strengthens the process by turning expert judgment into reusable evaluation data rather than one-off opinions.

To keep this workflow useful over time, focus on three things:

  • Govern the assets. Treat datasets, scorers, and evaluation runs as production artifacts. Version them, preserve lineage, and keep naming stable so results stay comparable over time.

  • Keep scorers focused. The best scorers do one job well. They measure a single dimension, use a clear scale, and lead to an obvious next action.

  • Turn feedback into data. User signals, developer review, and expert labeling should all feed back into the evaluation set, helping you catch regressions earlier and raise the bar over time.

When results regress, start with the trace. Check retrieval, tool calls, and response shaping before changing the prompt or the model. When metrics disagree, break results down by difficulty, scenario, or user segment before drawing conclusions. Evaluation should support judgment with evidence, not replace it.

The larger lesson is simple: offline evaluation and online monitoring should speak the same language. Reuse the same scorers where possible, measure the same quality dimensions before and after release, and make promotion decisions with both quality and operational trade-offs in view.
